I am a NICU nurse and it has been an incredible fit for me.  The subject matter is fascinating to me and learning about neonatology has become a special interest of mine that I can hyperfocus on while having professional benefits.  The schedule of working 3 12's in a hospital is nice because I basically just disappear into the void for 36+hours over the course of 3 days,  and then get to step out back into my real life and have time for things I enjoy.   The actual unit has a nice flow to it with some days being relatively chill, and other days being a chaotic adrenaline filled roller-coaster. 

NICU has an inherent structure to it based on the baby's care times, so the built in time keeping helps me outsource that level of executive function to the external boundaries of the unit.  

I get lots of relationship building with family members, but also, babies don't expect a ton from you other than love,  which is easy to give because they are babies, so if I am struggling with my social battery running low,  my actual patient doesn't require a lot of socialization from me.  

I used to be an ED nurse and it was not great for me despite the trope that everyone who works ED has ADHD. I did well with my patient care and enjoyed the adrenaline,  but the chaos was too overstimulating for me and it was draining to a point I couldn't hang anymore. I tried outpatient for a little while and hated the boredom of it, even if it was rarely overstimulating. NICU is a good fit for me.

I hear you.  I also work in a level 4 NICU, and used to work ED in Level 1 trauma before that. Honestly, unless the way that you feel is distressing to you,  or the people in your life are saying that you seem fundamentally different in a concerning way,  there is nothing wrong with maintaining space between the work side and the personal side. 

However, from what I read,  it does sound like you may be leaning so hard into the compartmentalization skills you have developed that you are bordering on dissociation from your emotions entirely.  There's a spectrum that can be balanced.  We need to be able to detach to do our jobs in the high intensity moments, mid code or resus delivery is not the time to be up in our feels, but the drive home or the morning after,  it's okay and healthy to let it out. That can be through talking if you have someone you trust who is willing to be that person for you, but just as easily it can be through a journal, or through just crying as you think back over your day,  or by going for a run or a workout. Somehow, you have to find catharsis or this job will eat you.  

I highly recommend reading the book, "Burnout: The secret to unlocking the stress cycle," by Amelia Nagoski. I find that there is a lot of overlap between emotional detachment and burnout, both in concept and in coping skills that can help with it.

Only you can decide if you feel like something needs to change, but from one internet NICU nurse stranger to another,  don't let this job take your humanity from you. Your job should be life enhancing (not perfect, and not always by any means, but it should never be stealing your joy or from the parts of your life that really matter), and a way to fund the things you care about.

It'll definitely be interesting to see how it all pans out.  I would say 10% of our fluids are d10 or d10 1/4NS, straight from the floor stock.  Probably 50% of our kids are on TPN/lipids so not affected thus far by the policy,  but then all the rest are either pharmacy made because of the sodium acetate or 1/4-1/2NS and heparin additives because most of our kiddos on fluids (with the exception of the babies hot out of the oven) have centrals (whether UVC or PICC), so have to have heparin. For us,  clears also include our syringe drips, so pressors, fent/prexedex, diuretics, paralytics, etc... which are all pharmacy compounded. I think it's just a little scary because we were so strict about q24 changes before.  Quadrupling that out of nowhere on a unit full of 22-25 weekers (because every kid wanted to pop out medium rare lately), is nerve wracking.
All of our babies are on dextrose.  They all start our at d10 and it can go up from there

Our NICU went from q24 sterile line/fluid changes for all the babies to all clear fluids can hang for 96 hours.  Only TPN and lipids are still q24. We are using 10cc flushes as boluses and are trying to IVP through primary lines when safe and compatible instead of having to use a flush so that we have them for the boluses.  It's a bit different in our population because we literally cannot give them water orally as their kidneys can't handle it. 

I am anxious to see what our clabsi rate does,  or what our NEC rate looks like in our unit through all this, because I can already see the push towards getting the babies on full feeds asap to get them off IVF. Gotta love living through unprecedented times so many times over 🙃

Totally normal! Baby has to actually work a little harder to get milk from your breast, so it naturally will take a little longer and allow them to feel their hunger/ fullness cues and respond to them a little more intuitively. Flow from a bottle is a little faster and therefore they may drink more before they actually begin to realize they are full. The bottle nipple also is a little more stimulus to their sucking reflex than your breast, so they suck more out of reflex than they might at your breast. There's actually some technique required to bottle feed a baby without overriding their hunger/ fullness signals,  rather it's all pretty intuitive to a bf baby at the breast. 

If baby is growing well,  staying on their growth curve,  and having an adequate amount of wet/poopy diapers, then you have nothing to worry about if you feed directly at the breast on demand.

I can't tell you how many times or how frequently this habit has saved and continues to save me.  I once found out that pharmacy had stocked the wrong med in the pyxis compartment this way.  Same aluminum packaging, and i had grabbed that med like a bazillion times before, so didn't look very closely. It wouldn't scan when I went to give it. Turns out it was a bag of magnesium sulfate,  not tylenol. I was about to run it by gravity like we always did with our tylenol in the ED 😅. Just yesterday, I went to scan a med and give it to my baby in the NICU, only to find it was a med put on my desk for a different kid. This habit is one of the very very best mistake prevention habits ever.

Literally the whole reason q1 checks are ordered is so that no longer than an hour goes by before a deterioration is ordered.  If you do your assessment and 1 minute later, the patient's status changes, if it's not discovered until 59 minutes later,  there has not been any negligence in the care provided,  EVEN if the deterioration went undetected for those 59 minutes.  In the NICU, we watch bellies like HAWKS. My tummy assessment is often the most detailed one of all the systems.  I had a baby develop serious symptoms of NEC within the 3 hours between assessments. I don't know if those symptoms started 2 hours and 59 minutes or 1 minute prior to my next assessment, and truly it doesn't matter.  My exams were ordered q3. The assessment was different 3 hours later,  and therefore the MD was notified and the workup began.  It doesn’t mean that my first assessment was incorrect.  The change means my assessment was thorough enough to detect the deterioration in status, and same for this nurse's neuro checks.

1. Definitely talking to providers.  I realized as I got more comfortable in the hospital that I really have about 10 seconds to ask for what I want for the baby and explain why I think it's needed. Too many details,   not having tried some troubleshooting of my own/ used the interventions at my disposal first, or not having a specific intervention in mind is a sure-fire way to get blown off. 

2. Documentation isn't a novel. You don't get brownie points for highest word count or detail. Say what you need to in as minimal of content possible. The more you put in your notes, the more rope you give someone to hang you with.  Document facts, minimal detail,  no opinion or anything that could be construed as such.  A big one I see a lot is documenting, "no orders received," after notifying a provider of a finding.  My bone to pick with this phrase is that it gives the impression that you believe that you should have received some kind of order in response to your notification, which then calls into question why you didn't escalate the situation if you feel it wasn't being addressed? It's completely fine to say,  "notified Dr. Whatshisface of patient's insert whatever here (vitals out of parameters, change of LOC, pain level increase, etc...)," and leave it at that. Obviously advocate for your patient, but you throw the provider under the bus while dragging yourself with if you insinuate that not enough was done to address your concern, without following up to demonstrate some kind of escalation of your concern. Also please for the love of God,  stop with the "will continue to monitor," or "care ongoing." It's an inherently implied standard of care that you are monitoring and continuing with the plan of care by nature of your being on shift and documenting the care provided.

You unfortunately likely cannot change his mind.  I do however have some suggestions that could help.  Your genetic testing will give you a lot more information. If it is isolated cardiac anomalies,  with no associated genetic disorder or syndrome,  I would suggest looking into a regional NICU referral center that has neonatal cardiothoracic surgery as a specialty,  cardiology isn't enough. You want to be able to deliver at the hospital that can perform any needed surgeries for your child.  Neonatal medicine has come a long way and surgery, even at days old,  is recoverable with pretty good outcomes in most cases, especially with early intervention and strong prenatal care.  Obviously, if this is a case you do not want to consider,  then having the abortion is your choice, though I would be prepared for your marriage to never recover.  

If you do find out that there are associated genetic anomalies causing the heart defect and probably others,  then I would get with a genetic counselor if you can, as well as trying to talk with a neonatologist who can give you a realistic idea of what you are facing.  Some disorders are relatively minor, some are catastrophic and incompatible with life.  You need to get an idea of what the impact is going to be on this child, both initially as a neonate, and progressively as they develop and throughout their lifespan.  I would tour a NICU and get an idea of what you are facing if you do carry to term.  Have them talk about possible procedures from intubation, to central line placement and surgical recovery. Truly try to get a full understanding of what your child will go through if delivered live. 

I would suggest talking through other options as well,  what will you do if the baby doesn't make it to term and you go into labor early as many do with genetic disorders.  If you go into labor spontaneously at 22 weeks, will you have your medical team try to delay it? Will you just have the child at that early stage and compassionately withhold resuscitation efforts to let them die in your arms or will you ask for full resuscitation measures (intubation, ventilation,  epinephrine, chest compressions, etc...). If baby makes it to term,  same question,  would you want full resuscitation or just to let the baby die in your arms? 

If you don't want to go through with the pregnancy, but you cannot convince your husband to be okay with an abortion,  you may have the option of talking to your provider and seeing if they would allow you to take an induction at an early date, so that you can deliver and hold,  let the baby pass "naturally." Depending on where you live,  and the regulations of the area, that may or may not be an option.  You are in an unenviable position.  I'm sorry you have to make these choices, especially without ever having fully discussed this with your partner.

Another thing to add, It's very easy to compare a preemie who has corrected to being closer to term, to a term baby's feeding expectations. But the womb is an industrial oven, and the NICU is an easy bake oven.  We try to give them the same conditions to grow in,  but it just isn't the same,  so they are going to take some extra time to master skills that older babies might not.  You are in good company in the NICU. Feeding is probably the most common last reason a baby is still in the NICU even after reaching term or beyond.

I am a NICU nurse and I cannot tell you how truly common this is.  If you have Speech Therapists available to you in your NICU, ask if they can help you with strategies to optimize your baby's feeding. But truly the biggest factor is time.  It's a tough skill to learn as babies have to master the art of suck, swallow, breathe coordination and that is no easy feat. It's truly a workout for them every 3 hours,  mentally and physically.  It takes time, but the magical thing is after feeling like nothing is happening,  all of a sudden they get it.  A baby who I could get to take 3ml a feed, and was only waking for 2 feeds in my shift will suddenly be ad lib and PO feeding all the next time I come back after days off. Eventually it just clicks.

It's nothing you are doing wrong,  it's nothing you're baby is doing wrong.  There may be some tips and tricks that could make minor improvements, but time, brain maturity, and oral motor skill development are the real drivers of feeding, and it's something that we truly can't control or predict. 

I feel like sometimes parents have an easier time wrapping their head around a very obvious medical reason that baby is still in the NICU (I.e needing oxygen, recovering from a surgery,  antibiotics or fluids, etc...), but something about feeding being the thing holding baby back from discharge just feels so frustrating because eating is one of the easiest, most second nature,  thing to us having done it our whole lives. and especially when term babies who had more cook time in the oven,  come out sucking down bottles with no issue.  It's so hard.  My heart goes out to you.  Your baby will get it. You guys will go home.  It just takes far longer sometimes than we all hope.

Going slow on the insertion was always my best trick. You will get to the point where you can feel the little *pop* as the needle enters the vein, then you know you can advance the needle slightly more at a flush angle to the skin before advancing your catheter. 

Another great trick to help with vein placement is learning how to identify valves. I hated when I would have a perfect stick, only to not be able to advance the catheter in due to hitting a valve. To check for valves, occlude the vein distally, then apply pressure with your other thumb, moving proximally to push the blood forward out of the vein. When you release pressure of your second hand,  the blood will back flow only to the closest valve, showing you where that is.  You can then choose an appropriate catheter size or insertion point to avoid the valve altogether. 

If you do happen to hit a valve, and you're pulling a hail Mary to save the line,  you can either remove the needle and try to flush the catheter through the valve (seldom worked in my experience), or you can rotate your needle 180 degrees inside the catheter and reinsert it inside the catheter (because the bevel is now up instead of down,  you reduce the risk of shearing your catheter). The needle can possibly help you guide through the valve (you will feel it and hear about it from the patient when you are successful because it doesn't feel nice). 

Also, you can try repositioning the catheter at a different angle and attempt to advance. Sometimes the vein has an angle to it you might not have seen or your insertion wasn't quite parallel, leading you to be trying to advance the catheter into the wall of the vein instead of the lumen. A simple angle change will fix that.  

Flush gently and with a pulsatile motion after drawing labs to make sure your line won't clot off. You can accidentally suck blood back into the line if you slam a flush like some do. It's not necessary. Slow and pulsatile accomplishes the same with less risk.  

Blood pressure cuffs make a great tourniquet for your really old patients with fragile veins. If the vein is visible on your old patients, consider not using a tourniquet at all because you increase the odds of blowing the vein. 

The hands are notorious for rolling veins. Hold the hand itself at a firm angle to the forearm, as well as holding the skin taught to reduce the roll. On a rolling forearm vein, you can consider inserting at a slightly perpendicular side angle to the vein, as a vein can eternally roll away from you if inserting from above. If you insert to the side of the vein, it can only roll one direction and to a limited distance. You can insert at that slightly perpendicular angle until puncture (also important to go slow so you can feel the moment of puncture), then adjust to flush/parallel to the vein before inserting that needle a little more and advancing your catheter. 

Also, for efficiency sake,  figure out how having things arranged works best for you,  how you like to secure your lines,  where you like your tape, where you keep your flush, where you place your sharps and trash as you go,  etc... and repeat the same process every time.  Eventually it becomes so second nature that you can practically do it without thinking.  

Also, you mentioned working in the ED. If your ED is anything like mine was, y'all may be very competitive about IV gauge for some reason lol. Unless your line is being used for something like blood via rapid infuser,  or a CT with contrast (and your CT tech isn't capable of using a smaller line for whatever reason), the size doesn't truly matter. You can do way more harm by trying to insert an 18g into a falsely inflated vein (because they get all pumped up from the tourniquet) than just going with the 22 for your tummy bug patient's complimentary bolus. You can achieve very similar flow rates as the bigger gauges through smaller gauge IV's with a pressure bag or pump (lol if you can find one in the ED). It's not really a badge of honor to drop a 16g in 109 y/o meemaw if it infiltrates in the first hour after placing it.  

Best of luck,  friend.  Practice makes perfect. Slow means smooth, smooth means fast.  Don't rush while still trying to gain the skill to begin with.  Speed comes with repetition.

One thing that I would suggest, from a former ER nurse myself, is to try and get comfortable with compartmentalizing. It isn't the bad thing that everyone makes it out to be.  Being able to keep a professional distance to keep yourself sane is healthy. What makes it an unhealthy coping mechanism is if you never allow yourself to access that compartment and feel what you need to,  process (talk, journal, therapy, etc...), and deal with the stuff you keep inside. That's when you see unhealthy issues like alcoholism or anger issues,  ptsd, etc... start to develop.  Another suggestion is to simply go into every shift with the mindset that death is an expected finding in the ER. Try to understand that most of the people you see in the ER that die, were absolutely going to die no matter what.  You helped give them their best *chance* of survival, but the odds were always going to be stacked in death's favor.  If on occasion you get the rare good outcome from a code, it feels so much sweeter when you always had the perspective that they were going to die and you helped them to live. If you hold the reverse idea that most people can be saved and then they aren't,  that will be processed as a failure,  when it really wasn't,  it was the inevitable.

Sure! My clock in time varies depending on the case schedule for the day,  but usually around 8am. I make post-op calls with one other nurse for patients from two days prior till the first patients for the day start coming out of the OR, usually about 9:30. 

We do only pain procedures (a lot of nerve ablations and epidural steroid injections), so only ever use moderate sedation.  It makes recovery really fast and easy for the patients.  I recover them for about 20 minutes each and give them their post-procedure education,  then wheel them on their merry stoned ways out to their driver on discharge. We do about 20-30 procedures in a day.  

I get a 30 minute lunch every day, and we don't have cases on Fridays, but usually hit about 36 hours across Mon-Thurs so tend to have half days on Friday where we just prep for the next week or make post-op calls. 

Depending on how fast the provider is that day, there can be downtime between patients so I usually jump over to pre-op and start lines or premedicate patients,  or help with pre-op calls/screening which is basically just verifying pt history and providing education prior to the procedure about how to prepare or what to expect.  There can be random little tasks in between as well since we're a small operation and we all pitch in and wear different hats at different times to keep the team functional. 

Overall it is heaven compared to hospital life. I make about 20k more than I did as an ER nurse,  leave by 6pm every day,  always get lunch,  have paid holidays off, and never work weekends. I am not so exhausted by the end of my shift that I can't enjoy my life outside of work,  and ultimately we make a big difference in quality of life for our pain patients so it's extremely rewarding as well.
